newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian aluminium imports to fall on budget levies.
newsitem.headline: Indian aluminium imports to fall on budget levies.

text.p: Indian aluminium imports are expected to fall sharply on proposals in the federal budget to raise customs duties on the metal, a move expected to help local firms cut their inventories, officials said on Monday.
"It will definitely help the domestic producers. (A) lot of imports will slow down," said Ashim Choudhury, executive director of the state-run National Aluminium Company (Nalco).
"It will be a major factor. It could cut imports by half," Choudhury told Reuters by telephone from the company's headquarters in the eastern Indian city of Bhubaneswar.
India imports about 60,000 tonnes of the metal annually.
In his 1997/98 (April-March) federal budget presented to parliament on Friday, Finance Minister P. Chidambaram raised the import duty on aluminium to 20 percent from 10 percent.
Analysts said the government decision would help integrated aluminium players but adversely affect companies which make extrusions and process the metal.
India has an annual production capacity of 670,000 tonnes of aluminium metal but output is much lower, forcing imports. It annually consumes around 500,000 tonnes of metal.
Apart from Nalco, Asia's largest aluminium producer, Hindalco, Indian Aluminium Co Ltd (INDAL) and Bharat Aluminium Co Ltd (BALCO) are the other major metal producers in the country.
Shares of leading aluminium makers rose sharply on the Bombay bourse after the federal budget proposed raising the import duty of aluminium.
Analysts said both Nalco and Hindalco were likely to increase the prices of their products in the coming months.
"It is benefical to the primary producers but it does not benefit the user industries," said INDAL deputy managing director Rana Philip. "There will be a cost push."
INDAL, the largest manufacturer of finished aluminium products in the country, annually produces over 50,000 tonnes and buys about 30,000 tonnes.
Industry officials said domestic aluminium producers had delinked their prices from London Metal Exchange (LME) prices last April, after they had begun to drop.
The domestic fabricating industry preferred to import the metal at cheaper prices rather than buy it locally and domestic producers were unable to liquidate stocks.
LME aluminium prices hit a two-year low in mid-October at around $1,300 per tonne.
Analysts said global aluminium prices had started picking up and with an increase in duties, imports would fast become unviable.
Choudhury said aluminium inventories had come down to about 25,000-30,000 tonnes from around 70,000 tonnes in November-December.

Analysts noted in the 1996/97 federal budget that the primary metal carried a 10 percent import duty while aluminium products had a 20 percent duty. In the 1997/98 budget both will carry a uniform 20 percent duty.
INDAL's Philip said the government should have increased the duty on finished aluminium products as base metal costs would go up.
